forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
question: How does the orchestra move from a crowded public dance to an ending in which almost nothing is left on stage?
intro: The evening fair is a succession of public dances interrupted by a private catastrophe. Its final pages refuse an ordinary ballet apotheosis: after the crowd disperses, muted trumpets let the supposedly lifeless puppet answer back.

sections.label: Back at the fair
sections.mNote: crowd rhythms return with renewed wind and brass weight

sections.label: The nursemaids’ dance
sections.mNote: folk melody passes through changing orchestral combinations

sections.label: Bear and merchant episodes
sections.mNote: a low tuba contrast gives way to brighter street dancing

sections.label: Coachmen and grooms
sections.mNote: heavy dance patterns accumulate voices and orchestral weight

sections.label: The masqueraders
sections.mNote: quick figures and repeated notes animate the masks

sections.label: Cries and pursuit
sections.mNote: the public dance breaks into fragmented theatrical action

sections.label: Death and dispersal

sections.label: Petrushka’s shadow

cues.title: Outside the puppet theatre again
cues.text: The last tableau returns to the public fair after the two private rooms. Winds, brass and strings restore collective movement; listen for the difference between a crowd’s continuing rhythm and the more unstable gestures of the puppets.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 96–103, rehearsals 82–89, begins with the curtain drum passage and Con moto crowd music. The report rises sharply from 0:00 to 0:05 and maintains strong activity through 0:35. This describes the opening span, not its first orchestral attack. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ballet made in months
cues.text: Stravinsky composed Petrushka between August 1910 and 26 May 1911. Its first performance followed on 13 June in Paris, with Pierre Monteux conducting: the complex fairground scenes were part of a new theatrical production, not a later suite assembled from separate pieces.
cues.evidence: IRCAM’s work record gives the composition interval, premiere date, venue and conductor. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Melody over a working bass
cues.text: The nursemaids’ dance sets a folk-like melodic line above busy bassoon figures and plucked string accompaniment. Keep the tune separate from the repeating mechanism beneath it; the accompaniment can remain active while the foreground sounds unhurried.
cues.evidence: Score p. 104, rehearsal 90, gives bassoon figures, violin fragments, pizzicato strings and then solo oboe. The changes at 1:04 and 1:08 lead into the quieter 1:10–1:35 span. Instrumental assignments are from the score. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune changes scale
cues.text: Within the nursemaids’ dance, a modestly scored tune can acquire the weight of a whole orchestral scene. Follow the growth across the phrase instead of assuming that a familiar melody must always keep the same instrumental identity.
cues.evidence: Rehearsals 90–99 expand and redistribute the dance. Relative level rises from −21.5 dB at 1:30 to −8.2 dB at 1:55 and stays strong through 2:25. The report supports the growth, not a specific handoff between instruments. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dance can withdraw
cues.text: The dance’s strong crest gives way to a much lighter passage before activity gathers again. Listen for this internal breathing space: the sequence is shaped by changing orchestral scale rather than by one unvarying folk-song accompaniment.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-evening.txt: a boundary at 2:30 follows the sustained 1:55–2:25 crest; the level falls to −23.0 and −24.1 dB at 2:35 and 2:40, then rises again. Score context: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka, rehearsals 90–99.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A familiar street song
cues.text: One melody in this dance is the Russian song commonly translated as “Down the Petersky Road”. Stravinsky did not invent all the fair’s tunes: recognition of borrowed material is one of the ways the ballet evokes a shared public world.
cues.evidence: Larner identifies “Down the Petersky” and its changing orchestration in the nursemaids’ dance. The cue names the source without claiming a particular statement begins at 3:00. https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Preparing another interruption
cues.text: The crowd music reaches another strong passage before a strikingly lower-centred episode. Compare the sound on either side of that change; Stravinsky can introduce a new act by changing register and accompaniment as decisively as by changing the tune.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-evening.txt: the 3:40 level crest precedes a boundary at 3:46 and the low spectral centroids of 3:50–4:25. The score introduces the peasant with bear at pp. 114–115: https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Pipe above a heavy animal
cues.text: For the peasant and bear, high clarinets represent the pipe while a tuba supplies the animal’s heavy movement. Listen to the separation of registers: the comic image depends on two very different kinds of motion sharing the same scene.
cues.evidence: Score p. 115, rehearsal 100, labels the action and gives high clarinets and tuba over low accompaniment. The report’s low overall brightness from 3:50–4:25 supports the approximate episode placement; it does not identify the tuba. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fair reassembles itself
cues.text: After the low-centred interruption, the fair’s more mobile texture returns and begins to grow. The sequence connects different attractions without pretending that they all belong to one continuous dance.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 116–120 returns to Tempo del principio before the merchant’s episode. The 4:34 change follows the low point at 4:35 and leads towards higher levels at 4:45–5:05. The stage entrance is not fixed to this cue. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Money enters the spectacle
cues.text: The scenario introduces a merchant with two women dancers; he throws money to the crowd and plays an accordion. The score represents that instrument rather than requiring an actual accordion, just as the puppet theatre represents its characters through orchestral voices.
cues.evidence: Kirchmeyer’s original-version structure, rehearsals 102–105, records the merchant, money and accordion. The original instrumentation contains no accordion. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A pause in the pressure
cues.text: A pronounced reduction in energy separates the street entertainments from the next heavy dance. Notice how little needs to change harmonically for a new group of people to seem to occupy the stage when the pulse and instrumental weight are reset.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-evening.txt: level falls to −23.8 and −27.3 dB at 5:55 and 6:00, followed by the strongest detected boundary at 6:08. The score’s new dance begins at rehearsal 108: https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf. No modulation is asserted.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A deliberately heavy dance
cues.text: The coachmen and grooms begin with a measured pattern in clarinets and horns over tuba, timpani and strings. The weight is rhythmic as well as low-pitched: listen for the repeated accents that let the dancers move as a group.
cues.evidence: Score p. 126, rehearsal 108, marks Moderato and pesante. The 6:08 boundary begins a lower-centred stretch, with a rise in level through 6:25. Placement covers the opening dance phrase, not its first accent. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More dancers, more layers
cues.text: As the nursemaids join the coachmen, the score adds further melodic activity to the heavy dance. Listen for accumulation rather than replacement: a pattern can continue while another group brings its own line into the same space.
cues.evidence: Score p. 131, rehearsal 112, explicitly marks the nursemaids joining, with clarinet and bassoon motion against the continuing dance. The analysis shows an ensuing rise towards the large 7:30–8:15 crest; the entrance itself is not bar-aligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The original orchestral palette
cues.text: This recording identifies the original 1911 orchestration. Stravinsky’s 1947 revision reduced and redistributed the forces; here the separate cornets, two harps and original keyboard colours belong to the earlier version, not an enlarged modern arrangement.
cues.evidence: The London CS 6009 cover says “Original Edition”; the original forces and later revision are described by Kirchmeyer and Larner. https://archive.org/metadata/lp_petrushka-complete-ballet-original-editio_igor-stravinsky-lorchestre-de-la-suisse-ro https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Masks replace the massed dance
cues.text: The coachmen’s accumulated weight gives way to the masqueraders’ quick-changing figures. Listen for the reduction at the join and the renewed activity that follows: a smaller beginning need not mean a calmer scene.
cues.evidence: Rehearsals 117–124 bring the masqueraders and repeated-note dances. The 8:26 boundary follows the large 7:30–8:15 crest; level then rises again through 8:45–8:50. This locates the episode broadly. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeated notes, restless movement
cues.text: Across the masquerade, short repeated notes and quick figures pass through changing groups. Listen to how a mechanically repeated gesture can gain urgency without becoming a long, singing melody.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 141–149, rehearsals 118–124, supplies repeated-note and running textures. The report measures high attack density at 9:00–9:10, reaching five onsets per second at 9:10. No particular repeated note has been aligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last public bustle
cues.text: The masquerade’s later passage alternates weight and quick activity instead of settling into a final cadence. Keep listening beyond the dance: its public continuity is about to be broken by the puppet theatre’s private conflict.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-evening.txt: changes at 9:34 and 9:48 precede the marked shift at 9:54, with renewed activity around 9:50. The scenario places cries and pursuit after the masqueraders, rehearsals 125–128: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A dance becomes a chase
cues.text: The music now follows cries, pursuit and the fatal blow rather than sustaining a public dance. Fragments and orchestral gestures carry the action; the chase’s short span will give way to an unexpectedly long, quiet aftermath.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 150–153, rehearsals 125–129, carries the cries, chase and collapse. The 9:54 change leads to a much lighter but high-brightness interval around 10:00–10:10, before the very soft 10:40 boundary. No blow is assigned an exact timestamp. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Small sounds after violence
cues.text: The death sequence uses soft high wind writing and muted strings instead of a grand funeral statement. Listen for the fragility of the remaining sound: the orchestra’s size is available, but Stravinsky withholds its mass.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 153–154, rehearsal 129, gives two piccolos, clarinets and muted strings, including divided violas. The report falls to roughly −33 dB at 10:40–10:50 and stays very quiet thereafter. Passage placement is approximate. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Only wood and sawdust?
cues.text: The Charlatan reassures the crowd that Petrushka is merely a puppet made of wood and sawdust. The stage story offers a rational explanation for what the audience has just witnessed, then prepares to undermine it.
cues.evidence: Kirchmeyer, Summary and original-version structure, rehearsal 130. This recounts the scene without timing the Charlatan’s first gesture to 11:24. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The crowd leaves gaps
cues.text: As the scene empties, short, quiet exchanges replace the fair’s overlapping bustle. Listen to the gaps between gestures; the ending creates room for one last voice by removing the crowd rather than by outshouting it.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 154–155, rehearsals 130–131, reduces the scene through low winds, muted horns and low strings. Relative level remains mostly below −24 dB through 11:35–12:20, with sparse detected attacks. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Muted trumpets answer back
cues.text: Petrushka’s shadow appears above the theatre. Two muted trumpets give the puppet another voice, piercing the thin texture rather than restoring the earlier orchestral mass. The Charlatan’s explanation has not secured the last word.
cues.evidence: Score p. 156, rehearsal 132, specifies metal mutes for piccolo trumpet in D and second trumpet in B♭. The report shows a new rise in level and brightness at 12:35–12:55. This is the approximate shadow passage, not its first note. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An ending without a triumph
cues.text: The final sound withdraws into sparse string gestures. This is the theatrical ending, not the optional loud concert ending printed elsewhere in the score: the last scene leaves the puppet’s status unsettled rather than turning his return into an orchestral victory.
cues.evidence: Score p. 156 closes with pizzicato strings; the separate alternative is printed as p. 150a. The report’s 13:02 change is followed by very low level through the 803.2-second endpoint, supporting the quiet theatrical close. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The crowd opens into a lighter dance
transitions.how: After the renewed crowd music, sustained wind chords and a reduction of orchestral activity prepare Allegretto. Busy bassoons and pizzicato strings establish a small accompaniment, into which violin fragments and the oboe melody enter. The handoff changes the scale of the scene while preserving its dance setting.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 103–104, rehearsals 89–90. The 1:04 and 1:08 changes follow the 0:50–0:55 crest and precede the quiet 1:10–1:35 interval. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: High piping meets a low tread
transitions.how: The score marks the crowd scattering as the peasant and bear arrive. Quick string figures give way to Sostenuto: high clarinets represent the pipe while the tuba’s low line moves against a steady accompaniment. The marked separation of registers and slower motion interrupt the preceding collective dance.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 114–115, rehearsal 100. The 3:46 change leads to low spectral centroids across 3:50–4:25. The report places the contrast; the score identifies pipe and bear. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Street flourishes give way to measured weight
transitions.how: The merchant’s quicker street-dance episode recedes before Moderato establishes the coachmen’s heavy pattern. Clarinets and horns begin above tuba, timpani and strings. A newly measured pulse and emphatic accompaniment distinguish the group dance from the preceding individual entertainments; no connecting modulation is needed to explain the handoff.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 126, rehearsal 108, follows the end of the merchant episode. Level reaches a low at 6:00 before the strongest detected change at 6:08 and a darker, renewed pattern. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Accumulated weight breaks into quick figures
transitions.how: The coachmen’s dance has accumulated the nursemaids and increasingly large orchestral forces. At the masqueraders’ arrival, that sustained weight is replaced by quicker wind and string figures, changing articulation and instrumental combinations. The join resets the texture rather than ending the fair’s activity.
transitions.evidence: Rehearsals 116–118 lead into the masquerade. The 8:26 boundary follows the 7:30–8:15 crest; relative level drops at 8:25 before renewed growth. No individual masked character’s entrance is aligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Cries interrupt the dance
transitions.how: The score breaks the masqueraders’ dancing with cries represented by muted brass. The ensuing chase uses short gestures and rapidly changing instrumental roles instead of maintaining the public dance’s repeating surface. This is a theatrical interruption: the puppets’ conflict forces its way into the fair without a conventional cadential preparation.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 150–152, rehearsals 125–128, documents the cries and pursuit. Changes at 9:48 and 9:54 lead to a much lighter, high-brightness passage around 10:00. The boundary estimates the sequence, not the first cry. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Violent motion collapses into quiet suspension
transitions.how: A string glissando and percussion gesture end the violent action. Lento replaces it with soft piccolo and clarinet writing over muted strings. The reduction is drastic: the public bustle is not resumed, and the remaining gestures make the death and the crowd’s uncertainty occupy a different scale of musical time.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 153–154, rehearsal 129. Relative level falls from −20.6 dB at 10:35 to −33.6 dB at 10:40–10:45. The passage estimate does not assign a timestamp to the fatal blow or dropped tambourine. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: A thin texture admits one last voice
transitions.how: The dispersing crowd leaves low, muted fragments rather than a closing tutti. Two trumpets with metal mutes enter for the shadow’s appearance, recalling Petrushka’s defiant character against the thin remaining texture. Their bright register makes the interruption decisive without restoring the orchestra’s earlier weight.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 155–156, rehearsals 131–132. The report’s relative level and brightness rise at 12:35 after the long soft aftermath, then fall again at the 13:02 change. Trumpet identity is score-derived. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 96–156, rehearsals 82–132; theatrical ending, not alternative p. 150a. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-evening.txt. Both harps share one stage position; piccolo trumpet remains under trumpets. Groups vary within each passage.

timeline.evidence: Score p. 104, rehearsal 90; changes at 1:04 and 1:08 followed by a quieter span.

timeline.note: High clarinets and low tuba represent the pipe and bear over a steady low accompaniment.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 115, rehearsal 100; 3:46 boundary and low spectral centroids through 4:25.

timeline.note: The merchant’s dance brings violin flourishes, oboe writing, harp patterns and plucked strings.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 120–121, rehearsals 103–104; relative level rises at 4:45–5:05 after the 4:34 change. Exact dancer entrance remains unaligned.

timeline.note: The coachmen’s opening pattern is deliberately heavy and measured.

timeline.note: The combined dance grows into a larger wind, brass and string texture.
timeline.evidence: Rehearsals 112–116; boundary at 7:42 inside the broad, high-level 7:30–8:15 crest. Groups are passage-level, not a simultaneous inventory.

timeline.evidence: Score pp. 140–144, rehearsals 117–120; 8:26 change before renewed growth and high attack density.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande (orchestra), Ernest Ansermet (conductor)
fields.note: Conductor and ensemble are printed on the sleeve and labels. No individual pianist, celesta player, harpist or other orchestral soloist is identified by the consulted carrier or reissue credits; those names remain unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The transferred London LP is expressly labelled Original Edition; Decca’s reissue catalogue corroborates Version 1911. The consulted full score represents that orchestration, not the 1947 revision. The exact early printing reproduced by Dover, and any session-specific corrections to players’ parts, remain unidentified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Decca discography entry S183[d] specifies 23–25 and 28 October, and 9 November 1957; the displayed value encloses these non-contiguous sessions. The HDTT reissue independently gives the same outer range. The individual tableau’s recording day and take dates remain unknown. Release and digitisation dates are not substituted for session dates.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Decca discography entry S183 and the reissue recording information explicitly name Victoria Hall, Geneva; the venue is not inferred from the orchestra’s home city.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying 1911 composition and original 1912 score are public domain in the United States; the ordinary EU life-plus-70 composition term has not expired.
fields.note: Stravinsky died in 1971, giving an ordinary EU term through 31 December 2041. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance, and it does not grant rights in modern editions, stage designs or choreography. fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established.
fields.note: A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
